title: Indoor soundscape, speech perception, and cognition in classrooms: A systematic review on the effects of ventilation-related sounds on students
review_question: How do sound stimuli related to the ventilation of the classroom (positively and negatively) influence students' learning and comfort?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Included: Field/lab studies recreating classroom, impact on speech perception/cognitive abilities/acoustic comfort, auditory/visual tasks for cognition, ventilation-related sound stimuli (MV/NV), chronic/acute exposure, journal articles after 1990 in English. Excluded: Pre-schoolers, hearing impairments, no subjective tests, manuscript unavailable, literature reviews.

findings.quote: A worsening in students' performance was consistently found as SNRs and STI decrease.
Two studies [64,73] investigated the effect of fan noise on language skills finding a negative effect on the students' performance.
No effect of the sound stimulus on mathematical abilities was detected.
as the noise level increased, students' attention decreased
significantly impaired the accuracy of the episodic memory task

Results showed a decrease in overall acoustic comfort [85] and pleasantness [80], and an increase in annoyance and disturbance [79] in presence of fan noise. A null effect on annoyance was also found... [86].
Chronic exposure to AN prompted a significant decrease in test scores according to four of the reviewed studies [51-53,55]
whereas Haines et al. [54] found no significant differences
simple reaction times and digit substitution tasks were not affected by AN [56,57,72], whereas the number of errors in attention switching increased [56,57].
Only episodic memory was found to be affected by AN, while no effects were consistently reported for all other memory types [50,53-57].
The studies consistently reported that students are annoyed by AN.

A decrease in comprehension performance with increasing TN level was found... Inconsistent results were also found regarding the effects of TN on reading time...
No consensus was found concerning noise effects on calculation accuracy, as both negative effects [68,70] and no effect [76] were reported.
the results showed no effect of TN on simple reaction time, digit substitution, and Toulouse Pieron task [55-57,72] while more errors occurred in the attention switching task [56,57].
None of the selected works showed negative effects due to TN. On the contrary, a positive effect (better accuracy) was found for informational and conceptual recall [50,55].

Consensus among studies was not found, as TN exposure was reported to increase annoyance [55,58,72,81,84], and disturbance [71], to have no effect [54,82], or even to provide a positive effect on the comfort domain [86].

Results showed a negative effect on episodic memory when construction noise was added

The noise of sirens was found to be detrimental to the acoustic comfort in three out of four studies [81,83,84], resulting in higher annoyance assessments. Exposure to construction noise was found to increase annoyance [79] and decrease pleasantness [86]. However, studies reporting none or little annoyance (null effect) on construction noise [81] and on construction noise and sirens [82] were also found.

The sound of children playing was found to negatively affect pleasantness [86] but not annoyance [82]. As regards the effect of noise from people in the street on the comfort dimension, either a negative effect [83] or a null effect [81] on noise annoyance was reported.
Both accuracy and response time improved in presence of rain sound.
After being exposed to NS, the students had shorter response times
The study showed that students were able to remember correctly longer series of digits when previously exposed to natural sounds.
NS were generally perceived as pleasant [80,86], not annoying [80], and able to provide a well-rated overall acoustic comfort [85].

synthesis_conclusions: Fan noise from mechanical ventilation consistently has a negative effect on speech perception, cognition, and comfort in classrooms.

Anthropogenic sounds (aircraft, traffic, railway, sirens, construction, human noise) entering classrooms via natural ventilation show mixed effects (negative or no effect) on student performance and comfort, depending on the specific task and noise characteristics.
Natural sounds from open windows consistently have a positive effect on students' learning and comfort.
Ventilation strategies can improve classroom soundscape depending on the outdoor context.
evidence_gaps: Low number of studies addressing specific cognitive sub-domains, with some results based on only one study.
MV-related noise levels tested often exceed recommended standards (e.g., baseline of 50dBA or more).
Lack of studies on the impact of aircraft noise on mathematical skills and speech perception.
Most studies on aircraft noise reported external, not internal, sound levels, lacking information on actual classroom exposure.
Insufficient data on arousal levels and spectral characteristics of traffic noise, and detailed urban context descriptions.
Paucity of studies on railway noise and sirens, preventing conclusions or patterns.
Lack of detailed information on levels and characteristics of outdoor human noise during subjective evaluations.
Heterogeneity of tasks and listening conditions across studies, preventing meta-analysis.
Incomplete reported data (e.g., sound levels, urban context, acoustic characteristics, baseline conditions).
Focus on normo-typical students, limiting generalization to vulnerable populations (e.g., L2 students, hearing impairments).
Lack of research characterizing dimensions underlying affective response to classroom soundscape to explore emotional and cognitive relationships.
heterogeneity_sources: Heterogeneity of tasks and listening conditions
Incomplete reported data (sound levels, urban context, acoustic characteristics)

moderators.effect: Lower temperatures strengthen the negative effect of fan noise on students' attention and memory.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Fan noise effect on attention was stronger at lower temperatures; longer response times for memory only at highest temperature.

moderators.effect: The effect of natural sounds on comfort is moderated by sound level, following a U-shaped relationship (higher levels associated with greater annoyance, maximum pleasantness at 45 dBA).
moderators.subgroup_effects: Greater annoyance and lower acoustic comfort at higher sound levels; maximum pleasantness at 45 dBA.

limitations: Review based solely on Scopus database, potentially missing relevant articles.
Inability to conduct a meta-analysis due to high heterogeneity in tasks and listening conditions across studies.
Incomplete reported data in original studies (e.g., sound levels, urban context, acoustic characteristics).
Inconsistent or incomparable baseline conditions used across studies.
Focus on normo-typical students, limiting generalizability to vulnerable populations (e.g., L2 students, hearing-impaired).

mechanism_chain.description: Ventilation-related sounds create a masking effect on speech signals, which increases the listening effort required by students, ultimately impairing their speech perception and comprehension in classrooms.
